You know, the regular order of the legislative system, the way it was designed to work is a committee goes to work to take a bill up like Farm Bill, they make amendments, they make changes, then they bring it to the floor. turn_text: Congressman Rick Berg, let's talk about North Dakota in general. What are the issues you think your state will face in the next few years that bother you?

Well, you know, I mean, things have been going very well in North Dakota. And I tell you, we've had some real dry spots and drought, but nothing like the rest of the country. And so, you know, the producers up here just want to let, you know, the other producers that taste a tough time, we hear them and concerned about them and just wishing them the best through the cycle. You know, I mean, there's no question that there's two huge threats that don't get talked about that much. Number one is the regulatory burden on agriculture. It's like almost every day you see people that are in a skyscraper writing rules who've never been, you know, wept to the Potomac writing rules for our farmers and ranchers and expect one size to fit all. I mean, that's one of the biggest risks that I think agriculture has is these regulations that come out with a lack of common sense. The other part of this would be the taxation. I mean, January 1, If nothing happens January 1, the estate tax, the death tax will go up to 55% on everything over a million dollars. I mean, it's just cuts right at the core of agriculture where, you know, part of our belief is trying to leave our farm and ranch to the next generation better than we received it. I had a five-generation farmer tell me, you know, we fought drought. We fought too much water. We fought disease. We fought market prices. But what's going to take us down is this fight against our own government with estate tax and regulations. So, I mean, that's one of the huge dangers we have facing agriculture.
